title: Tensile strength-ductility properties of face-centered cubic deformation twin/matrix structures
abstract: Abstract Large anisotropy of the tensile strength-ductility combination of the laminated twin/matrix (T/M) structure was found by studying the mechanical response of pre-twinned Cu-8at.%Al crystal structures, subjected to plastic tension under the different loading conditions. Three resolved shear stress-driven mechanisms, M 1 , M 2 , M 3 , were introduced to describe the deformation properties of the bimodal T/M structure. The “zero” tensile ductility (ε T ) accompanied by the tensile strength σ T  about 550 MPa or above 900 MPa was established when the T/M structure was loaded almost parallel (M 3 ) or perpendicular (M 1 ) to the T/M interface. Consequently, the T/M structure revealed the minimal (“zero”) tensile strength-ductility combination (σ T  × ε T ), when plastic yielding was initiated by M 1  or M 3  mechanism; both connected with T/M lattice shears occurring across the T/M interface. However, the T/M structure loaded at an angle about π/4 to the T/M interface revealed exceptionally large ductility (true strain equal to unity) accompanied by true stress of 850 MPa, i.e., the maximal combination σ T  × ε T  of 850 MPa, projected to about 1500 MPa for an analogous T/M structure of high manganese steels. All the “non-zero” cases of σ T  × ε T  were determined by activity of M 2  mechanism, i.e., T/M lattice shear parallel to the T/M interface. The σ T  × ε T  values depended on the length of M 2  deformation path terminated by a sudden entry of M 3  (M 1 ) mechanism. The entry, governed by the Schmid–Boas law, occurred always well before the Considère condition was met. The physical reasons of the observed anisotropy of the T/M structure are discussed.
journal: Archives of Civil and Mechanical Engineering

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Face-centered cubic (FCC) metallic materials may exhibit high tensile strength and simultaneously large ductility when mechanical twinning is involved during the plastic deformation process. Well-known examples of such materials are high manganese steels, called twinning induced plasticity (TWIP) steels. These steels reveal a remarkable value of the product between the ultimate tensile strength and the corresponding tensile strain, σ UTS  × ε UTS , [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 ,  4 – 5 ], much larger compared to that of non-twinned high-strength steels [ 6 ]. Mechanically twinned low stacking fault energy copper–aluminum alloys [ 7 ] or medium and high-entropy FCC alloys [ 8 ,  9 ] may also reveal the exceptional strength-ductility combination. There is a common agreement that the extraordinary tensile deformation properties are determined by the massive appearance of deformation twins within the grains of a heavily deformed—highly dislocated—polycrystalline material. However, as come from structural observations, the deformation twins, usually in the form of plates, are always interlayered by the non-twinned crystal regions, that naturally constitutes a well-developed laminated twin/matrix (T/M) microstructure. The laminated T/M microstructure is easily detectable by the electron back scattering diffraction technique of scanning electron microscopy (EBSD/SEM), as beautifully shown for instance in case of the high manganese steel deformed by tension at room temperature [ 10 ]. The T/M lamellae are often characterized by nano-scale thicknesses, as checked by transmission electron microscopy observations of the deformation twinning induced microstructures of different FCC materials [ 10 ,  11 ,  12 ,  13 – 14 ]. To conclude, we claim that to achieve proper fundamental understanding on the twinning induced plasticity of FCC materials an appropriate knowledge of crystal plasticity of the laminated, highly dislocated, T/M structures must be incorporated into consideration. Fortunately, such knowledge was very recently presented in the case of mechanically twinned single crystalline structures of the single-phase copper–aluminum alloy [ 15 ]. The advanced analysis of the experimental data reported in [ 15 ] shows that crystal plasticity of the laminated T/M structure of the copper–aluminum alloy is quite different compared to that created in the deformed material right before the entry of deformation twinning process. As established, the main physical reason for the difference is mainly associated with the massive appearance of the extended cube dislocations within the newly formed deformation twin regions. The analogous dislocation configurations should characterize the dislocation substructure of the deformation twins residing within the grains of the mechanically twinned polycrystalline materials. It is extremely important to emphasize that the “dislocation level” changes induced by deformation twinning appeared to be critical for the macroscopic mechanical properties of the laminated T/M crystal structures. To summarize the above discussion, any further experimental evidence on correlation between the cube dislocations-driven crystal plasticity and the deformation properties of the laminated T/M structures shall be very useful for better understanding of the twinning induced plasticity of FCC materials. Therefore, the main aim of the present paper is focused on the quantitative evaluation of the tensile deformation properties of pre-twinned Cu-8at.%Al crystal structure. Special attention will be paid to the anisotropy of the tensile strength-ductility combination. In particular, the transformations of fundamental deformation mechanisms, responsible for the minimal and maximal anisotropy of the strength-ductility combination of the bimodal T/M structure, will be established. As will be shown in the paper, the activity of the shear stress-driven deformation mechanisms of the bimodal T/M structure as well as their transformations are governed by the critical resolved shear stress law. An important yet unknown role of deformation detwinning on the tensile strength-ductility properties of the laminated T/M structure will be also established. The laminated T/M structure of the Cu-8at.%Al alloy was chosen to be studied here, because, as mentioned earlier, crystal plasticity of this structure was already well established [ 15 ]. Finally, it is also germane to note that quantitative empirical evaluation of the tensile strength-ductility properties of the laminated T/M structure was never yet reported in the literature for any FCC material.

sections.heading: Remarks on crystal plasticity of dislocated FCC twin/matrix structures
paragraphs: When bimodal T/M structure is subjected to tension, the resolved shear stress (RSS) of specific lattice shear system, i.e., one of the 48 possibilities, is predictable by a simple Schmid formula τ = σ × m, where τ is the RSS value, σ the amount of the tensile stress, and m the orientation factor of specific shear system, respectively [ 17 ]. The m, or alternatively τ/σ, may reach the value within the range of 0–0.5. It is useful to know which of the 48 lattice shears is the one mostly stressed for a given crystallographic direction of the tensile axis. Figure  2 a shows the K 1  plane perspective of 48 stereographic regions which are named according to the most stressed shear system of the bimodal T/M unit. Fig. 2 The K 1  plane stereographic map of the most stressed T/M double lattice slip and twin systems for a given orientation of the tensile axis ( a ) and the map of the T/M double lattice slip and twin systems of the highest value of orientation factor normalized by the critical resolved shear stress ( b ). See in Table  1  the crystallography of a given slip or twin system. Also note the insert in ( b ) where the stereographic regions of the T/M lattice shears of the M 1  group are magnified. The distribution of Schmid orientation factors ( c ) and their absolute values normalized by the critical shear stress, |m|/τ C  ≡ 1/σ Y  (d) of slip (CI T/M , CIII T/M , and CV T/M ), twin (C3 T  and C4 T ), and super slip (PI) systems of the T/M structure. The distribution is taken for the planar section marked by the great circle TD on ( b ). See more comments in the text

By means of Fig.  2 a we cannot predict correctly which lattice shear will operate for a given tensile direction in case of the dislocated T/M structure. This is because, according to the critical resolved shear stress (CRSS) law [ 17 ], a given shear system will be activated if the resolved shear stress τ will reach its critical value τ C  (τ = τ C ). In heavily dislocated crystal lattice of the T/M structure CRSSs of the K 1  and non-K 1  plane shear systems are quite different. Following the experimental data obtained in [ 15 ], CRSSs of all shear systems of the groups M 1  and M 3  (Table  1 ) can be evaluated as being about 250 MPa, whereas those of the M 2  group are approximately 100 ± 5 MPa; except for the twin shear C3 T  which is drastically smaller, being slightly above 55 MPa. Physical reasons of the extraordinarily high CRSSs of the non-K 1  plane slip systems (~ 250 MPa) and exceptionally low CRSS of the system C3 T , called as the π detwinning mode, were thoroughly discussed in [ 15 ,  18 ,  19 – 20 ]. For a comparison, the CRSSs of all lattice shears of the Cu-8at.%Al parent single crystal pre-deformed just prior to deformation twinning, differ by ± 15 MPa around the mean value of about 90 MPa [ 15 ]. This illustrates very well how drastic changes are induced by deformation twinning to the material’s plasticity during the M⟶T/M transformation process, i.e., the process where the single orientation matrix crystal region is replaced by the double T/M orientation structure. The predictions of which of the lattice shear of the dislocated T/M structure will operate at a given tensile crystal axis can be drawn from the fundamental relation of tensile plastic yielding, i.e., σ Y  = τ C /m, where σ Y , τ C , and m are the expected tensile yield stress, the CRSS, and the orientation factor of a given lattice shear system responsible for the plastic yielding, respectively. Following this relation, plastic yielding of the dislocated T/M structure loaded in tension will initiate by a shear system which has the lowest normalized CRSS, i.e., the CRSS value divided by absolute value of the orientation factor |m|; the absolute value of m is taken to make sure that the calculated value of σ Y  will be always positive. It must be remembered that activation of any twin shear in the matrix or twin layer must simultaneously satisfy the polarization condition of a lattice twin shear [ 21 ,  22 ,  23 – 24 ]. Of course, the criterion of minimal σ Y  is replaceable by the criterion of maximal 1/σ Y  value. Figure  2 b shows the K 1  plane map of the stereographic regions described according to the name of specific shear system satisfying the criterion of the maximal value of 1/σ Y  =|m|/τ C.  As observed in [ 15 ], twin shears of the matrix layer were practically not active at the tensile plastic yielding of the T/M structure. Therefore, the stereographic regions of C3, C4, and C11 twin shears are omitted in Fig.  2 b and consequently the corresponding data of m and 1/σ Y  in Fig.  2 c, d. Now, by means of Fig.  2 b one can predict which lattice shear of the dislocated T/M structure will satisfy the CRSS law for a given crystallographic direction of the tensile axis. There is no surprise that almost the whole stereographic projection is occupied predominantly by regions of the M 2  group lattice shears, including the biggest stereographic region of the shear system C3 T  of the lowest CRSS value. Compared with Fig.  2 a, the M 1  group regions are now limited to the small central part and to small ones located on periphery of the K 1  plane stereographic projection. The M 3  group regions, also located on the periphery, are noticeably reduced in size again at the expense of the regions of the M 2  group shear systems.

Correctness of the maximal 1/σ Y  criterion is also underlined in Fig.  2 , where a comparison between the values of m (Fig.  2 c) and the values of |m|/τ C  (Fig.  2 d) of the selected lattice shears are shown for a given planar section of the T/M structure, the latter marked by the great circle containing the pole “TD” (Fig.  2 b). Having crystal plasticity data of the dislocated T/M structure, one can easily predict the tensile yield stress σ Y  for each direction of the tensile crystal orientation, i.e., three-dimensional (3D) representation of σ Y  surface. As discussed earlier, the tensile yield stress σ Y  is predictable from the relation, σ Y  = τ C /|m|. The properties of σ Y  surface are convenient to show by means of the two-dimensional (2D) representations taken for three specific directions of the deformation twinning geometry, i.e., K 1 , η 1 , and S, respectively, the latter being the cross product, S ≡ η 1  ⊗ K 1  (Fig.  3 a–c). Fig. 3 The yield stress anisotropy of the T/M structure seen from perspective of the planar section perpendicular to the direction S ≡ η 1  ⊗ K 1  ( a ); the twinning direction η 1  ( b ) and the twinning plane K 1  ( c ).  d  The anisotropy of σ Y  corresponding exactly to the case of planar section marked by great circle “TD” in Fig.  2 b. Note that the radial distance between the adjacent circles is equivalent to 200 MPa. See more comments in the text

The data from Fig.  3 a, b show that the T/M structure of the Cu-8at.%Al alloy reveals extremely strong anisotropy of the tensile yield stress. The largest values of σ Y  are reaching well above 900 MPa along the direction perpendicular to the K 1  plane. This is when plastic yielding is controlled by activation of the M 1  lattice shear group. The lowest values of σ Y  are expected to be about 200 MPa or even 100 MPa, when plastic yielding is caused by activation of the M 2  slip or twin shears, respectively. The latter value relates to the C3 T  twin shear (π detwinning mode) occurring within the twin layer of the bimodal T/M unit. When the tensile yielding occurs by action of the conjugated slip shear of the M 3  group, the σ Y  values may reach on average the level of about 550 MPa. This is especially well seen for the K 1  plane section of the σ Y  surface which is totally controlled by properties of the M 3  conjugated slip systems (Fig.  3 c). In turn, Fig.  3 d shows the 2D surface of σ Y  corresponding exactly to the case of planar section (great circle “TD” in Fig.  2 b) which will be applied in this work to study the ultimate tensile strength and ductility of the pre-twinned Cu-8at.%Al single crystals. As concluded in [ 15 ,  20 ], exceptionally large CRRSs of the non-K 1  plane shears and hence remarkable σ Y  anisotropy of the laminated T/M structure result from the presence of the K 1  plane-extended cube dislocations [ 25 ,  26 – 27 ]. These very anisotropic configurations containing very wide stacking fault ribbons are extremely hard obstacles to be penetrated by the non-K 1  plane shears. According to the calculations performed in [ 15 ], the barrier stress needed for successful penetration of such obstacles may reach even 150 MPa. So, it largely contributes to the CRSS (~ 250 MPa) of the non-K 1  plane shears. These cube dislocation configurations are simultaneously responsible for the presence of the strong internal stress field targeted along the direction opposite to the primary twinning direction. The very advanced studies performed very recently in [ 20 ] showed that vanishing of the internal stress field down to zero, as expected near the limit of the thermal resistance of the T/M system, is accompanied by the decrease of CRSS of the non-K 1  plane shears from about 250 MPa down to about 120 MPa. The vanishing of the internal stress field was ascribed to the vanishing of the extended-stacking-fault configurations of the cube dislocations. Since the CRSS of the K 1  plane shear is about 100 MPa, the contribution of about 20 MPa only is expected to come from the barrier stress needed to penetrate the T/M interface. So, at room temperature the effect of the T/M interface shall contribute to the CRSS of the non-K 1  plane shears by less than 10% only. Therefore, as concluded in [ 20 ], transfer of plastic shear throughout the laminated T/M structure is predominantly controlled by the internal dislocation substructure of the deformation twins, not by the T/M interfaces. To summarize the above discussion, it is reasonable to expect that the exceptionally large anisotropy of the tensile strength and ductility of the laminated T/M structure, investigated here, will be largely controlled by the mechanical properties of the extended cube dislocations, not by the T/M interfaces.

sections.heading: Experimental
paragraphs: The pre-twinned parent crystals were served as a base material of samples designated for secondary tension tests. More than fifty secondary samples were cut out by spark cutter from the pre-twinned parent single crystals in eighteen different directions shown in Fig.  5 . Then, after careful mechanical and electro-chemical polishing the secondary samples of rectangular shape of about 30 mm in height and the cross section of about 1.5 × 2.5 mm 2  were subjected to secondary tension again at room temperature and the strain rate of 5 × 10 −4  s −1 . The CRRS of specific T/M lattice shear responsible for plastic yielding was calculated after the Schmid law formula, i.e., τ C  = Ϭ Y  × m, where Ϭ Y  was evaluated from the tensile characteristics and m from Fig.  2 c. That twin and slip shears of the T/M structure obey the CRSS law was already proven in the previous work [ 24 ]. Also, identification of specific T/M lattice shears responsible for plastic yielding was already done in [ 15 ] for identical set of secondary samples. Therefore, there was no need to repeat the same procedure here. Each experimental value of the critical stress was taken as an average of at least three independent measurements of Ϭ Y . Similar procedure was applied to evaluate the values of ultimate tensile stress Ϭ UTS  and ultimate tensile strain ε UTS . The corresponding physical quantities expressed in terms of true stress σ T  and true strain ε T  were calculated upon well-known relations: σ T  = Ϭ UTS  × (1 + ε UTS ) and ε T  = ln(1 + ε UTS ), respectively. To find physical condition controlling maximal value of the product σ T  × ε T , suitable microstructure observations, X-ray measurements of {111} pole figures, and other EBSD measurements were performed. Supplementary experimental procedures and analysis based upon the method of deformation gradient matrix were also applied; see the description later in the text. Fig. 5 Schematic representation of the secondary tensile samples cut out parallel to the lateral surface ND from the parent pre-twinned Cu-8at.%Al single crystal ( a ) in 18 different directions showed on the K 1  plane stereographic projection of the |m|/τ C  map ( b ). Note that the K 1  pole represents simultaneously the position of the T/M interface. So, for instance, the secondary tensile orientation axis of samples 1 and 18 are practically parallel, whereas those of samples 8–12 are largely inclined to the T/M interface

Finally, it is to emphasize that the dislocation substructure of all secondary samples of the tested T/M system is identical. The state of the dislocation substructure corresponds to the primary tensile deformation point, T/M, marked on the stress–strain curve of Fig.  4 a. So, all the mechanical data of the laminated T/M system presented later in this work are obtained for a given dislocation substructure. Activation of the slip or twin systems of the bimodal T/M structure does obey the rule of the critical resolved shear stress. For a given dislocation substructure, the critical stress of any slip or twin system is independent of the secondary tensile orientation axis and/or the orientation of the T/M interface, the latter shown by the K 1  pole position in Fig.  5 b. Therefore, the value of the Schmid factor is sufficient to establish all the tensile deformation properties of the bimodal T/M system. The Schmid factor values can be easily deduced from the specific pole position of the secondary tensile deformation axis (Fig.  5 b), when referred to the K 1  plane stereographic representation of the slip and twin systems shown in Fig.  1 c.

sections.heading: Results and discussion
paragraphs: Examples of engineering stress (σ E ) versus engineering strain (ε E ) curves of the secondary samples loaded by quasi-static tension at room temperature along different directions of the planar section ND (Fig.  5 ) are shown in Fig.  6 a, b, whereas Fig.  6 c, d shows the same mechanical properties but expressed in terms of true stress (σ) versus true strain (ε). For clarity, the whole collection of the obtained tensile characteristics is limited to representative four cases numbered 1, 4, 7, and 9 (Fig.  6 a, c) and another four cases numbered 10, 12, 14, and 16 (Fig.  6 b, d). Fig. 6 The engineering stress–engineering strain curves of selected secondary tensile samples numbered 1, 4, 7, and 9 ( a ) and 10, 12, 14, and 16 ( b ). For clarity, the curves of samples 9 and 10 are in the inserts located at upper right corners. The true stress–true strain curves of selected secondary tensile samples numbered 1, 4, 7, and 9 ( c ) and 10, 12 14, and 16 ( d ). For clarity, the curves of samples 9 and 10 are in the inserts located at lower right corners

When plastic yielding occurs by PI mode (M 3  group of the T/M lattice shears), a large mechanical instability (dσ/dε < 0) is observed at the very beginning of the tensile deformation (e.g., curve 1). The instability is caused by heavy strain localization developing rapidly into the neck and finally leading to a sample failure. In such cases ultimate tensile stress σ UTS  and the true stress σ T  are taken as being equal and both equivalent to the yield stress σ Y  (σ UTS  = σ T  = σ Y ). Consequently, the values of ε UTS  and ε T  are both evaluated as equal to 0.02, i.e., to the amount of plastic strain ascribed usually to initial tensile plastic yielding. When ε UTS  increases, the ratio between σ T  and σ UTS  also increases following the relation: σ T /σ UTS  = 1 + ε UTS . The values of σ UTS  and σ T  differ remarkably when plastic yielding occurs by the M 2  group of T/M lattice shears and particularly significant differences between them are observed for modes CIII T/M  (sample 7) and CI T/M  (sample 12). The differences between σ UTS  and σ T  are well seen when mechanical characteristics of Fig.  6 a, b are compared to their correspondences in Fig.  6 c, d. In practice, σ T  is equal here to maximal value of the true stress. This is because the mechanical stability of the tensile test is always lost rapidly (e.g., curve 4 or 16) or extremely rapidly (e.g., curve 9 or 12) due to the entry of catastrophic strain localization leading immediately to sample failure. All numerical data drawn directly from the stress–strain characteristics (σ Y , σ UTS , ε UTS ) and those calculated ones (τ C , σ T , ε T , σ UTS  × ε UTS , σ T  × ε T ) as well as the T/M double lattice shear modes responsible for plastic yielding of the secondary samples are provided in Table  2 . The experimental results are also shown graphically in terms of the orientation dependence of σ Y , σ UTS , and σ T  (Fig.  7 a), σ UTS –σ Y  and σ T –σ Y  (Fig.  7 b), ε UTS  and ε T  (Fig.  7 c), as well as σ UTS  × ε UTS  and σ T  × ε T  (Fig.  7 d). Figure  7 a shows how σ Y , σ UTS , and σ T  depend on the crystallographic directions of the tensile axis of the planar section ND marked in Fig.  5 . The conjugated slip mode PI (M 3  group) and the M 2  group shears, i.e., detwinning modes C3 T  and C4 T  and slip modes CI T/M , CIII T/M , and CV T/M , are all contributing to the 2D surfaces of σ Y , σ UTS , and σ T  (Table  2 , Fig.  7 a). For the sake of simplicity, a very narrow CV T/M  space of orientation is omitted on Fig.  7 . The superscript “T/M” is used here to emphasize that the slip modes may operate in twin and matrix layers of the T/M structure simultaneously. The planar anisotropy of σ Y  is extremely large because CRRS of the mode PI (~ 255 MPa) is by a factor of 2.5 larger than CRSSs of other accessible shear modes of the group M 2  (~ 102 MPa); except the case of mode C3 T  (CRSS equal to about 55 MPa), where the ratio of τ C (PI)/τ C  (C3 T ) is even over 4.7 (see the data of τ C  collected in Table  2 ). The orientation dependence of σ Y  showed here was already reported in [ 15 ], where the physical origin of this exceptional σ Y  anisotropy was thoroughly discussed. The angle position of main axis of a sample is measured clockwise from the zero-angle position ascribed to sample 14. The shear mode of sample 11 is described as CI T/M *, to emphasize that detwinning mode C4 T  was also partially contributing to the whole tensile deformation path.

The main goal of the present studies was to examine how these initial strengthening properties of the T/M structure may change at most during subsequent plastic tension, i.e., when the amount of plastic strain corresponding to the ultimate tensile strength will be accumulated in the tested material The strengthening effects of σ Y  ⟶ σ UTS  and σ Y  ⟶ σ T  is well seen when 2D surfaces of σ UTS  and σ T  are compared to the σ Y  surface. As mentioned earlier, for the range of orientation of the PI mode the strengthening effect measured by the difference of (σ UTS –σ Y ) or (σ T –σ Y ) is in both cases evaluated to zero (see the corresponding values of σ Y , σ UTS , and σ T  in Table  2 ). Surprisingly, the effect measured by the difference of (σ UTS –σ Y ) is extremely small and practically negligible when the M 2  lattice shears are brought into operation (compare surface σ UTS  and σ Y  in Fig.  7 a). This effect is still very weak even if exceptionally large amount of plastic strain (ε UTS ) was accumulated in a deformed sample (see the tensile characteristics numbered 7 or 12 in Fig.  6 a, b and the corresponding numerical data provided in Table  2 ). The situation changes dramatically when the effect of tensile strengthening is evaluated by the difference of (σ T —σ Y ) which allows to reveal the work hardening potential of the T/M structure (Fig.  7 b). It appears that the initial level of the tensile strength (σ Y ) may increase almost four times during the whole tensile deformation path (σ T  corresponding to ε T  of about 1.0); see the tensile stress–strain curve 12 in Fig.  6 d and the corresponding numerical data for the sample 6 in Table  2 . Since differences between σ UTS  and σ Y  are small, 2D surface (σ T –σ UTS ) is plotted in Fig.  7 b instead. The anisotropy of the (σ T –σ Y ) and (σ T –σ UTS ) surfaces is beautifully reflected by the anisotropy of the ε T  or ε UTS  surfaces shown in Fig.  7 c. It simply means that tensile strengthening potential and ductility of the T/M structure are totally integrated with each other. The T/M structure can increase its own strength by tension only when the T/M lattice shears of the group M 2  will be activated. The strength-ductility integration—combination—is finally shown in Fig.  7 d, where 2D orientation dependences of the products σ UTS  × ε UTS  and σ T  × ε T  are plotted. Figure  7 d shows extremely large anisotropy of the σ UTS  × ε UTS  and σ T  × ε T  surfaces with their maximal values observed for the CI T/M  and CIII T/M  range of orientation of the tensile axis. The strength-ductility properties of the T/M structure were drastically lower when the tensile deformation occurred by detwinning modes C3 T  and C4 T  (see the stress–strain curves 9 and 10 and the corresponding mechanical properties shown in Table  2 ). This important aspect of the tensile strengthening properties of the T/M structure will be discussed later. Consequently, zero values of these products are ascribed to the PI orientation space. To conclude, the maximal strength-ductility combination of the T/M structure was fully controlled by the deformation conditions allowing as much as possible for activity of slip-type modes of the M 2  lattice shears (e.g., CI T/M  and CIII T/M ). What are these deformation conditions? By asking more generally, what controls the ultimate tensile strength and ductility of the T/M structure on any given direction of the tensile axis. To answer this general question let us first establish the physical reason limiting maximal strength-ductility combination of the T/M structure obtained here for the samples 8 and 12 (see values of the products σ UTS  × ε UTS  and σ T  × ε T  in Table  2 ). To find physical nature of the limit, supplementary experimental procedure was introduced to carefully monitor deformation properties of the T/M structure during the whole CI T/M  and CIII T/M  tensile strain paths. Of course, special attention was paid to the deformation point (ε UTS , σ UTS ), where the entry of catastrophic strain localization and finally the sample failure occurred. Slip line observations and X-ray measurements shown in Fig.  8  confirmed that plastic yielding of sample 12 begun with entry of CI T/M  lattice shear of the highest 1/σ Y  value, as predicted in Fig.  2 d. X-ray measurements of {111} type pole figures taken at ε = 0.55 and ε = 1.01 allowed to identify rotation path of the tensile axis during the entire tensile deformation of sample 12. It appeared that rotation of the tensile axis occurred almost exactly on the great circle from pole 12 toward the pole [011], i.e., toward the shear direction of CI T/M  slip system (Fig.  9 a). It means that CI T/M  slip system totally dominated the whole path of the tensile deformation of sample 12. Analogous set of experimental data confirmed that plastic yielding of sample 8 begun and continued up to the point of ε UTS  by operation of CIII T/M  lattice shear. Note in Fig.  9 a rotation path of the tensile axis of sample 8 occurring along great circle between the poles 8 and [101], the latter being the shear direction of CIII T/M  slip system and in Fig.  9 b X-ray data of inverse {111} pole figures, which confirmed stability of the T/M structure up to the end of tensile deformation (ε UTS ) of sample 8. Fig. 8 The patterns of slip lines identifying activity of the CI T/M  slip plane at the initial plastic yielding of sample 12, seen on lateral surface ND ( a ) and the surface perpendicular to the direction TD ⊗ ND ( b ). ( c ) Corresponding crystallographic analysis after X-ray measurements of {111} pole figures Fig. 9 ( a ) The types of the tensile axis rotation path, “8 ⟶ [101]” and “12 ⟶ [011],” showed on the suitable part of K 1  plane stereographic projection of Fig.  5 b after X-ray and SEM/EBSD measurements of {111} pole figures. Rotation of the tensile axis of samples 8 and 12 was additionally checked at intermediate stages of tensile deformation, ε = 0.9 and ε = 0.55 (marked on the figure). Rotation path of the type “10 ⟶ [112]” of sample 10 up to the deformation point of ε UTS  is also shown; ( b ) X-ray data of inverse {111} pole figures taken at the very end of the tensile deformation (ε UTS ) of sample 8

The CI T/M  deformation path of sample 12 was also checked by measuring geometrical changes of initial cross section, taken at ε = 0.55 and ε = 1.01 The obtained data are summarized in Fig.  10  (see insert located at left upper corner). Having experimental data on rotation of the tensile axis (Fig.  9 a) and applying the method of the deformation gradient matrix one can easily establish that transformation of the initial cross section of sample 12, observed at ε = 0.55 and ε = 1.01 (Fig.  10 ), would require to produce by CI T/M  slip system an amount of simple T/M lattice shear of about γ = 1.37 and γ = 3.15 respectively. In turn, the CI T/M  deformation matrix method predicts the angle between the lateral surfaces of the sample accumulated the amount of crystal lattice shears γ = 1.37 and γ = 3.15 as equal to 64.2° and 44.8°, respectively. These calculated values of the angles fit extremely well compared to those measured experimentally at the tensile deformation of ε = 0.55 and ε = 1.01, respectively, as shown in Fig.  10 . As appeared, such enormous amount of lattice shear accumulated in sample 12 before the tensile instability (Fig.  10 ) was possible mainly because of two reasons; (I) the initial crystallographic position of the tensile axis; (II) CRSS difference between CI T/M  slip system and any other slip system of M 1  or M 3 , as suitably implemented on 1/σ Y  map of the K 1  plane stereographic projection (Fig.  9 a). The critical question is what happened at the end of tensile deformation able to stop the CI T/M  slip system from continuing its operation? To answer this question, careful structural observations (SEM/BSE) and crystallographic measurements of {111} type pole figures (X-ray) were performed in advancing neck (see the insert located at low right corner of Fig.  10 ). Also, the strengthening capacity, i.e., the ratio between the work hardening rate dσ/dε and the current flow stress σ, was evaluated right before the tensile instability point (σ = dσ/dε). Fig. 10 The work hardening rate dσ/dε and true stress σ versus true strain ε of sample 12 deformed by quasi-static tension at room temperature. Note huge strengthening capacity (dσ/dε)/σ > 1.5 of the deformed sample right before the tensile instability point (dσ/dε = σ). Note insert (left upper corner) showing optical microscopy pictures of the sample cross sections taken at ε = 0.55 and ε = 1.01. Note insert (right lower corner) showing schematically places of the advancing neck marked by 1, 2, and 3, where suitable X-ray and SEM observations (see the data in Fig.  11 ) were made to identify transformation of plastic deformation mechanism of CI T/M  → PIII, i.e., M 2  → M 3  type, responsible for the loss of the tensile stability

The mechanical analysis revealed valuable information that the tensile instability was premature, i.e., it started far before the Considère criterion was met (dσ/dε > 1.5). In turn, the sequence of structural observations revealed that at the same point of the tensile deformation CI T/M  slip system was replaced by the new super slip system PIII (see intense CI T/M  slip in Fig.  11 a replaced by very intense “wavy” slip taking place on the composition plane (P ≡ A/A T ) in Fig.  11 b). Considering that twin lamellae occupy about 90% of the total volume of the T/M structure, the composition plane must lie much closer to the position of the plane A T  compared to plane A of the matrix lamellae. This situation is beautifully reflected in Fig.  11 d, where crystallographic position of the plane P found after the {111} pole figures analysis is shown. It is important to realize that the (P) plane contains only one slip direction, III≡[101], parallel to the intersection of three slip planes of the T/M system, i.e., A of the matrix layer, A T  of the twin layer, and the T/M interfacial plane K 1  (Fig.  11 d). Such situation constitutes a collinear set of super slip involved in further development of necking (see “wavy” lines along the composition plane caused by conjugated AIII ∪ AIII T  super slip and large activity of C/C T  lattice shear in Fig.  11 c). To conclude, premature tensile instability or alternatively the ultimate tensile strengthening properties (σ UTS , ε UTS ) of sample 12 were controlled by the CI T/M  → PIII changeover of the dominant deformation system, or more generally, the M 2  → M 3  transformation of simple shear mechanism of the T/M structure (Table  1 ). That the tensile instability may occur far before the Considère criterion is met was already proved for the case of soft oriented FCC single crystals [ 29 ]. Premature tensile instability was always observed when conjugate slip or twin system took over primary slip at the end of overshoot [ 30 ,  31 ,  32 – 33 ]. The changeover of slip–slip type was also carefully studied quantitatively for Cu [ 34 ] and Cu–Al [ 35 ,  36 ] single crystals. It can also be induced by discontinues change of the tensile deformation path. As concluded in [ 24 ,  35 ,  36 ], the changeover was governed by CRSS law and it was always associated with heavy localization of plastic strain developing to necking (slip–slip) or Lűders type deformation (slip–twin).

The CI T/M  → PIII transformation observed here is another case of the changeover occurring in the bimodal T/M structure at the ε UTS  point of the tensile deformation, where CI T/M  slip is replaced by the conjugated super slip AIII ∪ AIII T . Assuming the CI T/M  → PIII changeover is also governed by CRSS law, at the point of ultimate tensile strain of sample 12 the ratio between critical stresses of CI T/M  and the PIII slip systems must be equal to the ratio of their Schmid factors, i.e., τ C (CI T/M )/τ C (PIII) = m(CI T/M )/m(PIII). At the point of ε UTS , m values of CI T/M  and PIII slip systems were evaluated for the current crystallographic direction of the tensile axis (Fig.  9 a) as equal to 0.26 and 0.39, respectively. Now, CRSS of CI T/M  slip system can be evaluated after the relation, τ C (CI T/M ) = σ T  × m(CI T/M ), i.e., τ C (CI T/M ) = 845 MPa × 0.26 = 219.7 MPa. Consequently, CRSS of PIII super slip system was equal 329.6 MPa, i.e., τ C (PIII) = τ C (CI T/M ) × (m(PIII)/m(CI T/M )). According to predictions of 1/σ Y  map (Fig.  9 a), the “12 ⟶ [011]” rotation path should be stopped not at the ε UTS  point of the tensile deformation, but later, when intersecting the boundary between CI T/M  and BIV stereographic regions. It means due to CI T/M  → BIV changeover. The fact that this hypothetical CI T/M  → BIV changeover was eliminated from activity means that at the ε UTS  point CRSS of BIV slip system had to be greater than 407 MPa. The experimental data show that CI T/M  plastic tension can increase the strengthening properties of PIII and BIV slip systems by a factor of 1.5 and at least by 1.6, respectively. This strengthening is quite understandable, because of the large effect of “forest” hardening of non-K 1  plane lattice shears PIII and BIV, which should result from enormous activity of the T/M lattice shear (CI T/M ) parallel to the K 1  plane. However, it is extremely interesting that the CRSS of CI T/M  slip system changes during its tensile deformation path even more intensively, i.e., by a factor well over 2. Considering that m factor of the CI T/M  system decreases from the initial value of 0.46 down to 0.26 at the end of the tensile deformation, the expected effect of “pure” geometrical hardening consists of an increase of the initial tensile stress of 215 MPa up to about 380 MPa only, whereas a major part of σ T , i.e., 845–380 MPa = 465 MPa, would have to be ascribed to a real work hardening effect. This observation is extremely intriguing; however, further physical explanation to this is beyond the scope of the present paper. Finally, due to CI T/M  plastic tension, the initial ratio τ C (PIII)/τ C (CI T/M ) = 2.5 decreases significantly taking at the ε UTS  point the value of 1.5. Taking all the above into account, it is obvious that 1/σ Y  map shown in Fig.  9 a must be corrected according to the changes induced by CI T/M  plastic tension to crystal plasticity of the deformed T/M structure. Following the correction, at the ε UTS  point the tensile axis of sample 12 should lie exactly on the boundary between CI T/M  and PIII stereographic regions. Simultaneously, the adjacent BIV stereographic region should be removed from the 1/σ Y  map. Similar analysis of the tensile strengthening data of sample 8 led to the following information: (I) he premature tensile instability resulted from CIII T/M   → PI changeover of the dominant deformation system; (II) CRSS of CIII T/M  lattice shear has increased by a factor of 1.54 (99 → 152 MPa); (III) CRSS of super slip system PI (M 3  group) and slip system BII (M 1  group) has increased only by a factor of 1.06 (255 → 270 MPa) and 1.21 (255 → 309 MPa), respectively; and (IV) the increase of the tensile strength of sample 8, σ Y  → σ T  (210 → 632 MPa), resulted from geometrical (202 MPa) and work hardening (220 MPa) effects, simultaneously. Due to CIII T/M  plastic tension the initial ratio, τ C (PI)/τ C (CI T/M ) = 2.6, decreases also significantly taking at ε UTS  point the value of 1.8. Again, 1/σ Y  map (Fig.  9 a) must be corrected according to the changes now induced to crystal plasticity of the deformed T/M structure by CIII T/M  plastic tension. The strength-ductility combination (σ T  × ε T ), observed for CI T/M  plastic tension of sample 12 (845 MPa), rapidly decreases as the initial tensile axis takes successively the position of sample 13 (440.9 MPa), 14 (140.1 MPa), and 15 (98.4 MPa). As shown in Table  2 , this is accompanied by a drastic decrease of ε T , which equals 1.01, 0.71, 0.29, and 0.19, respectively. Such a sequence of events is readily understood once we realize that accordingly, the angular distance from the initial position of the tensile axis to the boundary between stereographic regions of CI T/M  and PI (sample 13 and 14) or eventually CI T/M  and PV (sample 15) decreases also significantly (Fig.  5 b). On the other hand, high strength-ductility combination (σ UTS  × ε UTS  or σ T  × ε T ), observed for CI T/M  and CIII T/M  plastic tension of sample 8 and 12, decreases suddenly in the intermediate range of orientation of the tensile axis (Fig.  7 d). This was observed for the case of samples 9 and 10 (see corresponding numerical values in Table  2 ). As checked after X-ray measurements of {111} pole figures and independently by SEM/EBSD observations, the plastic tension of sample 10 was “as much as possible” controlled by another type of M 2  lattice shear, i.e., the detwinning shear mode C4 T . The activity of C4 T  detwinning mode, called also as π/3 detwinning [ 20 ,  37 ], was identifying after the two following experimental data obtained: (I) the “10 → [112]” type rotation path of the tensile axis, checked at ε = 0.2 and at the point of ε UTS  (Fig.  9 a) and evaluation of cumulative thickness of twin and matrix lamellae; the data revealed total recovery of matrix orientation regions occupying now about 97% of total volume of the T/M structure deformed up to the tensile strain ε ≈ 0.2 (Fig.  12 ). To fully eliminate twin lamellae from the T/M structure, i.e., to complete the reverse (T/M → M) transformation, an additional amount of tensile deformation would require to be accumulated in the deformed T/M structure. This situation was carefully checked for C11 T  tensile deformation path (also the π/3 detwinning mode) in [ 19 ], i.e., for the quite similar case to the C4 T  tensile deformation path investigated here. The term “as much as possible” used above means that C4 T  tensile deformation path is limited and must end as soon as the reverse, T/M → M, transformation will have been completed. Considering that twin lamella contributed about 90% to total volume of the initial T/M structure, the correspondence matrix method [ 21 ,  22 ] predicts that the T/M → M transformation should be completed at ε ≈ 0.26. So, further tensile deformation up to ε T  = 0.45 (Fig.  6 d; Table  2 ) concerns heavy dislocated single orientation structure (M) without the T/M interfaces present any longer. The position of the tensile axis of sample 10 checked after X-ray measurements at ε UTS  (Fig.  9 a) indicates that “10 → [112]” rotation path was kept up to the tensile instability point. It means that the subsequent duplex slip, involving most stressed symmetrical CI and CIII slip systems of the resultant shear direction [112], was replaced at the ε UTS  point by non-coplanar lattice shear, i.e., BII or BIV slip system. This can be easily deduced by referring “10 → [112]” rotation path of sample 10 to the data of 1/σ Y  map (Fig.  2 b) showing stereographic regions of the most stressed slip systems of the matrix crystal lattice. Fig. 11 Slip line markings of PIII super slip system seen on the lateral surface ND of sample 12 at different stages of neck formation ( a–c ). The stages are marked schematically in the insert of Fig.  10  by points 1, 2, and 3, respectively; ( d ) shows corresponding crystallographic analysis after X-ray measurements of {111} type pole figures. Note the trace of the composition plane (in red) occupying the position between the traces of the planes A T  and A of the twin and matrix crystal lattice, respectively. See related comments in the text Fig. 12 SEM/EBSD picture of sample 10 deformed up to ε ≈ 0.2 of the true tensile strain. Note total domination of the matrix region occupying almost whole volume of the T/M structure. The cumulative thickness of the twin lamellae is less than three percent of that of the matrix lamellae. Note also pictures of {111} type pole figures taken locally in the “pure” matrix region (the upper insert) and in the region containig also the remaining twin lamellae (the lower insert)

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: The experimental results obtained in this work on the pre-twinned Cu-8at%Al crystal structure allow us to draw some important conclusions concerning the tensile strength-ductility properties of laminated T/M FCC structures. The yield stress σ Y  of the pre-twinned Cu-8at%Al crystal structure, evaluated at ε Y  = 0.02, was extremely anisotropic. It may change even by one order of a magnitude with a change of orientation of the tensile axis, i.e., from about 100 MPa, when plastic yielding is initiated by π detwinning (K 1  plane lattice shear), up to even above 900 MPa when a non-K 1  plane lattice shear is brought into operation. The σ Y  anisotropy data of the pre-twinned Cu-8at%Al single crystals fully confirmed those reported in the recent work on crystal plasticity of the laminated T/M FCC structures [ 15 ]. The ultimate tensile strain ε UTS  of the pre-twinned Cu-8at%Al crystal structure was also extremely anisotropic. Depending on the orientation of the tensile axis, it changed from the value of the engineering strain ε E  = ε Y  = 0.02 (ε UTS  ≡ ε Y ) up to even ε E  ≈ 1.8 (see the corresponding data in Table  2  for samples 1, 16–18 and 6–8, 12, respectively, and the stress–strain curves of samples 1, 16, and 7, 12 in Fig.  6 a, b). These large changes of ε UTS  were accompanied by surprisingly small changes of the tensile strengthening effect, as measured by the difference between the ultimate tensile stress σ UTS  and the yield stress σ Y . Irrespective of the orientation of the tensile axis used, the difference (σ UTS –σ Y ) did not exceed 100 MPa (see the data shown in Fig.  7 a). However, when the same tensile strengthening effect was measured by the difference between the corresponding true stress and the yield stress, i.e., (σ T –σ Y ), it changed substantially with a change of orientation of the tensile axis, i.e., within the range of 0–630 MPa (Fig.  7 b). Depending on the orientation of the tensile axis, the strength-ductility combination of the pre-twinned Cu-8at%Al crystal structure, expressed numerically as the product σ UTS  × ε UTS , changed from about 11 MPa (ε UTS  = ε Y  = 0.02) up to about 530 MPa (ε UTS  ≈ 1.8). When expressed by the product σ T  × ε T , it changed from about 11 MPa (ε T  = ε Y  = 0.02) up to about 850 MPa (ε T  ≈ 1). The lowest values of the strength-ductility combination, associated with the effect of “zero” tensile ductility (ε UTS  = 0.02), correspond to the tensile orientations practically parallel to the T/M interface (see the data of the samples 1, 17, and 18 in Table  2  and their tensile orientation positions inclined to the normal direction to the T/M interface (K 1 ) by about π/2, as shown in Fig.  5 b). The observed maximal values of the strength-ductility combination (e.g., the samples 6 and 12) correspond to the tensile orientations largely inclined to the T/M interface (see the near π/4 zone angular distances of “6⟶K 1 ” and “12⟶K 1 ” in Fig.  5 b). If the T/M structure was loaded when tension axis was parallel or almost parallel to the T/M interface, it revealed the effect of “zero” tensile ductility accompanied by relatively high level of true tensile stress of about 550 MPa. Plastic yielding was initiated by the M 3  type lattice shear, i.e., a conjugated T/M lattice shear occurring simultaneously on the two-twin orientated non-K 1  planes along the common K 1  plane slip direction (see the crystallography of the M 3  type mechanisms in Table  1 ). If the T/M structure was loaded when tension axis was largely inclined to the T/M interface, it revealed the effect of “large” ductility, accompanied by extremely high level of true tensile stress reaching even about 850 MPa at the true tensile strain of about unity. Plastic yielding was initiated by the M 2  type lattice shear, i.e., a T/M lattice shear occurring on the K 1  plane shear along the K 1  plane slip direction (see the corresponding data of samples 6 and 12 in Table  2  and the structural observations and crystallographic measurements shown for sample 12 in Figs.  8  and  9 ). Taking advantage of the experimental data on compression of the laminated T/M structure of Cu-8at.%Al alloy [ 15 ] and assuming the expected symmetry of the tensile/compression yield stress, the T/M structure loaded by tension perpendicular or almost perpendicular to the T/M interface is expected to reveal the effect of “zero” ductility (catastrophic strain localization into shear bands at the very initial plastic yielding), accompanied by extremely high level of the yield stress, i.e., above 900 MPa. Plastic yielding was initiated by the M 1  type lattice shear, i.e., a T/M lattice shear occurring on the non-K 1  plane along the non-K 1  plane slip direction (see the crystallography of M 1  type mechanisms of the bimodal T/M structure shown in Table  1  and the predicted anisotropy of the tensile yield stress σ Y  shown in Fig.  3 a, b). The M 2  type tensile deformation path of the T/M structure was always terminated by entry of M 3  (M 1 ) or type T/M lattice shear. The entry always induced premature tensile instability and led to a heavy strain localization and finally to sample failure. The M 2  ⟶ M 3  (M 2  ⟶ M 1 ) transformation does obey the critical resolved shear stress law. To illustrate the conclusion, see the mechanical data of the M 2  type deformation path and the tensile instability of sample 12 shown in Fig.  10  and the associated structural observations and crystallographic measurement shown in Figs.  8 ,  9 , and  11 ). The mostly stressed M 2  type lattice shears of slip type (see the crystallography of the M 2  type mechanisms shown in Table  1 ) determine large tensile ductility of the T/M structure (see the data of samples 6–8 and 12 in Table  2  and the stress–strain curves of sample 7 and 12 in Fig.  7 ). Large activity of the M 2  type slip systems resulted in substantial increase of critical stresses of all types (M 1 , M 2 , and M 3 ) of T/M lattice shears. The mostly stressed M 2  type lattice shears of detwinning type (see the crystallography of the mechanisms C3 T , C4 T , and C11 T  in Table  1 ) substantially reduced the tensile ductility of the laminated T/M structure (see for instance the stress–strain curves of sample 9 an 10 in Fig.  7  and the corresponding data in Table  2 ). So, detwinning significantly restrains the strength-ductility combination of the laminated T/M structure (see the data shown in Figs.  7 c, d). As postulated, exceptional tensile strength-ductility combination of the laminated T/M structures results from physical properties of K 1  plane-extended cube dislocations contributed substantially to the dislocation substructure of the deformation twin lamella.
